newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Australia's Great Barrier Reef faces starfish plague.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Australia's Great Barrier Reef faces starfish plague.

text.p: The kaleidoscopic coral and tropical fish are hypnotic as you glide over the Great Barrier Reef powered only by your flippers, but what often fails to catch your eye is a dull brown, nasty-looking starfish.

The coral-eating Crown of Thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci), however, is again attacking the world's largest reef system, and scientists predict a significant loss of coral. Growing up to one metre (three feet) in diameter and armed with sharp spines tipped with powerful toxin, the Crown of Thorns crawls across the reef eating coral polyps.
The starfish can digest its body diameter in colourful polyps daily, leaving behind bleached coral skeletons, protected by its toxic spine from natural predators.
AT HOME ON THE REEF
In the early 1960s the Great Barrier Reef was attacked by millions of Crown of Thorns, killing one fifth of the 2,600 reefs which stretch 2,500 km (1,550 miles) along Australia's northeast coast.
Film of the reef at the time showed large clumps of colourless, disintegrating coral, abandoned by marine life.
Attempts by Australian naval divers to kill the starfish by injecting it with toxic copper sulphate had to be stopped as the heavy metal toxin entered the food chain.
It took 10 years for the first plague to pass.

Starfish numbers exploded again in the late 1970s and early 1980s. But by 1990 the Crown of Thorns, a natural species in coral reefs dating back 7,000 years, had mysteriously disappeared, with only two detected in a 400 km (250 mile) section of the Great Barrier Reef.
THE STARFISH RETURNS
But two years ago Australian marine scientists monitored a build up of juvenile Crown of Thorns in the north of the reef and predicted a fourth outbreak when the starfish matured and reproduced.

Those Crown of Thorns are now mature and are beginning to reproduce, with females delivering up to 100 million eggs at a time. The eggs can float hundreds of kilometres (miles) before settling on a reef.

"If we assume these cycles are very, very similar, then you can expect quite significant loss of coral cover for some areas this time around," says Udo Engelhardt, the head of the Crown of Thorns research at the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority.

Surveys in the past two years have found a significant number of Crown of Thorns on 24 reefs stretching from Lizard Island in the northern section of the Great Barrier Reef to the tropical city of Cairns.
Their population is now three to eight times normal levels, with the highest concentration up to 380 per hectare, says Engelhardt, adding a sustainable level is around 30 per hectare.
The outbreak will peak on reefs offshore from Cairns, but plagues are not uniform and while some reef outcrops can be devastated, others may remain unscathed, he said.
COPING WITH THE CROWN OF THORNS
The marine park authority has decided to try to control only local outbreaks of the starfish if they pose a significant danger to a particular reef or tour operation, says Engelhardt.
Divers will inject the Crown of Thorns with the biodegradable toxin Sodium Bi-sulphate, also known as dry acid.
"Without knowing why the outbreaks occur it would be stupid to try and knock off all the starfish. We don't know what effect it may have on the reef eco-system," says Engelhardt.
Scientists are at a loss to explain why the Crown of Thorns outbreak occurs, but some believe man is responsible.

"Some people seem to be convinced this is an entirely natural phenomenon -- just a cycle between starfish and coral," says Engelhardt. "Others argue there is possibly some human intervention in these cycles and that it may be caused by human activity."

Engelhardt said those who argue the latter blame over-fishing of the starfish's natural predators, the Giant Trident Shell and two fish species, along with an increase in soil-borne nutrients washed into the ocean from coastal farms.

The nutrients stimulate growth of algae which nourish the Crown of Thorns. Tens of thousands of tonnes of nitrogen and phosphate are washed from coastal sugar farms onto Australia's Great Barrier Reef each year.
"But there is no definitive evidence one way or the other," says Engelhardt.
Scientists are also mystified as to why parallel outbreaks of the Crown of Thorns occur in the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
Engelhardt says the current Australian outbreak mirrors recent outbreaks in South Africa, the Red Sea, Fiji, the Solomon Islands and the Cook Islands.
"There seem to be systematic outbreaks across two oceans," says Engelhardt.
